titel: Seasoning and caring for cast iron
kurz: The black layer on cast iron and carbon steel pans is not dirt but oil that was bonded into a hard, smooth layer at high heat. It protects against rust and makes food stick less.
bild_im_kopf: Like a varnish you bake on yourself: every thin coat makes the surface smoother.
was_passiert: When a very thin film of oil is heated past its smoke point, the fat [[molekuel|molecules]] link up into a solid network, a kind of plastic. This patina bonds to the iron and fills its pores. Cast iron is heavy and conducts heat rather poorly: it heats slowly and unevenly. In return it stores a lot of heat and barely cools when searing.
warum_wichtig: Well seasoned, an iron pan sears steaks with a crust no non-stick pan can match, and it lasts a lifetime. Badly cared for, it rusts and everything sticks.
faustregeln: For a smooth patina: many thin coats instead of one thick one, because thick oil stays sticky.
Preheat for ten minutes on medium heat before searing, because cast iron heats unevenly.
Cook long acidic braises with tomato or wine in an enamelled pot instead, because acid attacks the patina.
schritte: Wash the pan and dry it completely on the hob.
Rub in a teaspoon of neutral oil and wipe almost all of it off with kitchen paper: it should look matt, not oily.
Heat it upside down in the oven at 230 to 250 °C for an hour, then let it cool in the oven.
After cooking, rinse it hot, dry it on the hob and oil it very thinly.

mythos.behauptung: Cast iron must never touch washing-up liquid.
mythos.richtig: A well-seasoned patina is firmly bonded and can take a little washing-up liquid. Soaking and leaving it wet do the damage, because the iron then rusts.
